title: Wood for boxes and small furniture
subtitle: Choosing seasoned timber for joinery, what cuts well, what stays flat, what finishes cleanly
excerpt: Seasoned timber for boxes and small furniture needs to satisfy three conditions: it must cut cleanly under hand tools, it must stay flat and stable once joined, and it must finish well with oil or wax. This guide covers the right species for each type of small project, how to read a board for stability, and what to avoid.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the timber selection guide; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the stability and finishing guide.

glossaryTerms.definition: Timber sawn so that the annual rings run roughly perpendicular to the face of the board. More stable than flat-sawn and less likely to cup or bow in use.
Timber sawn through the log in parallel slices, so the annual rings run roughly parallel to the face. Cheaper to produce than quartersawn but more prone to movement.
The tendency of timber to shrink or expand with changes in humidity. High movement timbers are unsuitable for close joinery without allowance for the movement.

content.text: For small boxes, racks, trays, and furniture pieces made with hand tools, the right timber is not the hardest or the most expensive, it is the one that saws straight, planes cleanly, takes glue well, and stays flat after the piece is made. The species that satisfy all four conditions are a short list. The species that look right but move badly or tear under the plane are also a short list, and they come up frequently because they are widely available.
Species that work well
Oak
The most versatile hardwood for small furniture. White and English oak both plane and saw well, finish beautifully with oil, and have low
movement
when
quartersawn
. A quartersawn oak board is recognisable by the medullary ray flecks (silver streaks) on the face.
Flat-sawn
oak can cup across the width over time. Source quartersawn where possible for boxes and trays.
Ash

Pale, straight-grained, and outstanding in tension, which is why it is used for tool handles, coat racks, and anything subjected to repeated loading. Ash planes cleanly with the grain and sands quickly. Finishes pale with oil; good for pieces where a light colour is wanted. More movement than oak but still manageable in normal indoor conditions.
Cherry

The finest native hardwood for small decorative boxes. Cherry darkens with UV exposure to a warm red-amber over several months. It planes to a very smooth surface and finishes beautifully with wax or oil. More expensive than oak or ash; best used for pieces where the timber itself is a feature. Low movement.
Walnut

Dark, stable, and finishes the best of any common hardwood with oil. Walnut is harder than cherry but planes more easily because the grain is straighter. The dark colour means every joint and surface flaw shows, walnut is not forgiving of poor workmanship. Best for pieces where dark colour is wanted and the work is careful.
Species to avoid for jointery work
Elm: high movement and interlocked grain tears badly under the plane. Good for turnings; not for flat boards.
Chestnut: beautiful grain but very high movement; splits easily if not allowed to move in the joint. Not for enclosed boxes.
Softwood (pine, spruce): good for beginners' boxes (soft, easy to cut) but dents in use. Not for functional kitchen pieces.
Reading a board for stability

On the end-grain of a board, read the annual ring arc direction. If the arcs curve away from the face of the board (quartersawn orientation), the board will stay flat. If the arcs curve toward the face (flat-sawn), the board will try to cup toward the face as it dries out. A slight cup is manageable with a plane; a severe cup means the board will split a joint if glued flat.
Sourcing in the UK
Local sawmills: the best source for native hardwoods. Many will cut to order and will advise on stability and grain direction.
Reclaimed timber dealers: old oak boards and shelving make good box timber, already dry.
Online timber merchants: specify quartersawn where available. UK suppliers include John Boddy's, Roger Coupe, and Vastern Timber for native hardwoods.
